questions.question: Before reading the lesson: which property does a good agent eval verifier need above all others?
options: Determinism across runs, so the same candidate output always produces the same verdict
Speed in the millisecond range, since the eval suite must run inside a tight CI budget
A natural-language explanation of the verdict that a human reviewer can read without digging into logs
Coverage of every line of the candidate's code, similar to a unit-test coverage report
questions.explanation: Determinism is what makes a regression detectable. A non-deterministic verifier turns every red into a coin flip — speed, prose explanations, and code coverage don't solve that problem.

questions.question: A candidate scores 3 passes in 5 samples on a single task. What value does the lesson's pass@5 formula return (rounded to two decimals)?
questions.explanation: pass@k = 1 - (1 - p)^k = 1 - (1 - 0.6)^5 = 1 - 0.4^5 = 1 - 0.01024 = 0.98976, which rounds to 0.99. This is the lesson's simplified formula, treating each sample as an independent Bernoulli trial with pass probability p; it approximates but is not identical to the unbiased estimator from Chen et al. 2021 (pass@k = 1 - C(n-c,k)/C(n,k), computed exactly from n total samples and c correct ones). The raw per-sample rate (0.6) — not the amplified pass@5 value — is what the 0.60 option names directly.

questions.question: Why does the lesson include both pass@1 and pass@k in the report?
options: pass@1 is the number shown to users in the dashboard, while pass@k is kept for internal debugging only
pass@k can hide a model that is right only one in many samples, so pass@1 anchors the result to first-attempt quality.
pass@k and pass@1 are mathematically identical whenever k is greater than 1, so reporting both is redundant
pass@1 is the version supported by the verifier registry; pass@k is reserved for future verifiers.
questions.explanation: pass@k makes models that get the answer once in many tries look strong; pass@1 is the first-attempt floor. Reporting both prevents over-claiming — they are not dashboard-vs-debug variants, nor mathematically identical, nor a registry limitation.

questions.question: The harness calls _prepare_scratch before every sample. Why is that important for pass@k > 1?
options: It avoids race conditions that would occur if multiple sample runs shared the same temp directory concurrently
It ensures each sample starts fresh from the buggy setup, not from the previous sample's leftover output
It is purely a performance optimisation that has no effect on the correctness of any individual sample's verdict
It is only relevant when the verifier being used happens to be a shell-based exit-code verifier
questions.explanation: Without a fresh scratch, sample N+1 starts from sample N's output. The harness would measure 'second-attempt cleanup' rather than first-attempt success — it is not about concurrency, performance, or a specific verifier type.

questions.question: You add a new verifier 'pytest_passes' that runs pytest in the scratch dir. Which existing verifier should you base it on?
options: file_equals, because pytest can be configured to write a JSON results file after the run completes
regex_match, because the text output from a pytest run contains the literal word 'passed' somewhere
shell_exit_zero, because pytest signals success by exiting the process with code 0
It is impossible to express a pytest run as a verifier, since pytest has no machine-readable output at all
questions.explanation: pytest exits 0 on pass and non-zero on failure. shell_exit_zero is the right primitive. Production wiring routes the call through the sandbox from lesson 26.

questions.question: A reviewer asks: 'is this regression in the model or in the harness?' Which artifact answers that question?
options: The per-task, per-sample SampleResult together with the verifier's detail message for each run
The agent's chain-of-thought transcript, since it records the model's reasoning for each sample
The verifier registry source code, since it defines how every verdict is computed
The fixture JSON files, since they define the buggy setup each sample starts from
questions.explanation: Per-sample latency, verifier detail, and pass/fail let you triage: same fixtures, different verdicts, so the model changed; same verdicts but different latency, so something else moved.
